summary: Rhode Island's Fuller Rock Light: an 1872 wooden tower on a granite pier in the Providence River, destroyed in 1923; the pier still carries an automatic light.

lens.where: original 1872 lens, fixed white at first

structures.note: Granite pier begun 1871 under contract; the present light stands on the same foundation

structures.type: hexagonal wooden pyramid with cast-iron lantern
structures.note: Fourteen feet tall; destroyed by explosion and fire on 5 February 1923
Erected on the old foundation after the 1923 fire; lantern at about 40 feet (LighthouseFriends) or 50 feet (Bulletin) above the water
Twenty-foot light tower installed by the Coast Guard when the pier was refurbished

access.note: On a granite pier in the Providence River channel; the sources describe no visitor access

events.note: Congress appropriates $20,000 for three lights above Sabin Point: Pomham Rocks, Fuller Rock and Sassafras Point
Fourteen-foot hexagonal wooden pyramid tower with cast-iron lantern on the granite pier
Sixth-order Fresnel lens; fixed white light at first
Lorenzo D. Clark hired 11 July 1872 at $320 a year; removed in November
Board secures $5,000 to buy a site and build a keeper's house; no site found in 1875 and 1876; the house was never built
Wooden towers show considerable decay; the Board requests $1,000 for cast-iron towers, not funded
John J. Mullen appointed at $550 a year
Pier repointed, cavities filled with concrete, seventy-five tons of riprap added around the base
Color of light changed on 27 June 1900 (white to red, per LighthouseFriends)
Converted to acetylene and run unmanned; flashes every three seconds (LighthouseFriends); around 1918 per the second history
Sassafras Point light discontinued in July after dredging removed its shoal (the pair's other light; LighthouseFriends)
Acetylene tank explosion and fire on 5 February 1923 during servicing by the tender Pansy; several crew injured, none seriously
Steel skeleton tower erected on the old foundation; Providence paper reports the new tower within an afternoon, lantern 50 feet above the water (Bulletin); LighthouseFriends says forty feet
Coast Guard refurbishes the granite pier, adds 25 tons of riprap, and erects a new 20-foot tower

corrections.proposed: granite pier begun 1871 (standing); wooden hexagonal tower of 14 ft (4.3 m), built 1872, destroyed 1923; steel skeleton tower 1924; present 20-ft tower, 1997
corrections.why: The 1872 wooden tower was destroyed by an explosion and fire in February 1923 (Bulletin; LighthouseFriends). The 4.3 m figure is the height of that wooden tower, so the record describes a structure that no longer stands. The standing tower dates from 1997 on the same pier.
The 1923 explosion destroyed the light, but a new tower was raised on the same foundation in 1924 and the light kept showing. It was not deactivated.
An automatic solar-powered light operates on the pier today (New England Lighthouses), and LighthouseFriends says a modern light is shown from the old foundation.
The Coast Guard refurbished the pier and installed the present tower in 1997 (LighthouseFriends; New England Lighthouses).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Two dates for two structures on one granite pier. The pier and the first light date from 1871-1872 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends). The 1997 tower is the current structure (Wikidata's 1997 is the present tower only).
OpenStreetMap's 'standing' matches the present light and pier. USLHS 'lost' fits the 1872 wooden tower, destroyed in 1923.

notes_for_editor: Printed pages were not read: the Board's 1900 entry is scan page 21 of annualreportlig00statgoog; the Bulletin entries are PDF pages. DISAGREEMENTS NOT SETTLED: (a) lantern height of the 1924 steel tower: 40 ft (LighthouseFriends, 'twice the previous height') against 50 ft (Bulletin reprint of the Providence Evening Bulletin, 2 December 1924). (b) Automation year: 1912 (LighthouseFriends; Bulletin 1912 list) against around 1918 (New England Lighthouses). (c) Light height at first: 28 ft above mean high water (LighthouseFriends) against 14 ft tower height and 17 ft on an early light list (New England Lighthouses); the USLHS place record gives focal height 26.0 ft. The record's focal_height_m 9.4 (ENC) is not checked. (d) Characteristic: 'Iso R 6s' in the record matches the present three-second red flash alternating with three seconds of darkness (New England Lighthouses); the 1912 'flashes every three seconds' wording (LighthouseFriends) is not reconciled. (e) Keeper names: Clark is spelled Clarke once (New England Lighthouses); Heard is spelled Hurd by the roster. Joseph Pollard appears only in the roster. (f) LighthouseFriends names an acting keeper, Ed Grogan, in February 1912, who is not on the USLHS roster; left out of the roster for want of a dated primary record. (g) Mullen's rescue is secondhand: LighthouseFriends says it was taken from a Providence Journal article; the Journal was not read. The story says so. (h) The Mullen dating 'New Year's Eve in the 1890s' is LighthouseFriends' wording; no year is given. (i) Same-name confusion: the Coast Guard and LSS records for 'Fullers Rock' that appear in the LSS annual reports (1905, 1898 letter) refer to a rock off Hunniwells Beach, Maine, not Rhode Island; not used. (j) Chronicling America: two RI hits for 'Fuller Rock' lighthouse, 1872-1923 (1881 Narragansett Herald; 1895 Providence News, a party of young men near the light); neither used. (k) The Boston Globe report of 1923 (quoted by LighthouseFriends) was not read. (l) Access: the sources describe no visitor route; the story says not to land or climb. (m) NRHP and any state register: not checked. (n) The USLHS place coordinates (41.7898, -71.3748) sit about 0.6 km from the record position (41.7941, -71.3797), within the roster tool's name-and-position match. (o) 'Channel Light 42' appears only as a record name; not checked. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28: LighthouseFriends' references list a 1936 Providence Journal piece, but its text ties the Mullen rescue only to 'a Providence Journal article'; the story no longer names which one, and the Journal was not read. No visitor access to the pier is recorded in any source read; the story says only that no visitor access is recorded. Height disagreements are now stated in the story: 26 ft (USLHS) against 28 ft (LighthouseFriends, New England Lighthouses); tower 17 ft on an early light list against 14 ft in later lists. The 1924 lantern height stays as 40 ft (LighthouseFriends) against 50 ft (Bulletin reprint). The 1900 Board entry (scan 21, annualreportlig00statgoog) was confirmed with corpus.py page; the Bulletin PDF pages were confirmed by their text.
